# About Root3D

**Hardening the Cannabis Supply Chain from Seed to Sale.**
Agriculture. Science. Technology. Business. Real-World Execution.

## Mission
Root3D is a multidisciplinary agricultural, cannabis, technology, and business consulting firm. We combine scientific research, commercial cultivation, facility engineering, compliance, cybersecurity, automation, and commercialization under one roof.

## Philosophy
We are practical problem-solvers, not generic consultants selling templates. Our work is honest, accessible, and scientifically grounded. We diagnose the problem, implement the fix, document the result, and put safeguards in place so it does not happen again.

## Why four disciplines
Operational failures in regulated agriculture rarely stay in one department. A restriction in an irrigation line changes how the plant feeds. That shows up in the lab results, which shows up in the compliance report, which shows up in retail margins.

Root3D was built around that chain. Joel works the inputs and the chemistry, Danny works the canopy and the infrastructure, Dusty works the data, the documentation, and the storefront, and Hunter works the rules, the molds, and the devices. Together we cover seed to sale, and we talk to each other so you do not have to translate between specialists.

## What we value
- **Honest answers.** If we are not the right fit, or the fix is cheap and simple, we will say so on the first call.
- **Evidence before opinions.** We look at your data, your plants, and your paperwork before recommending anything.
- **Teach, do not just tell.** Your team should understand why a change works, so they can run it without us.
- **Write it down.** Every engagement ends with documentation you own: what we found, what we changed, and what to watch.
- **No guarantees we cannot keep.** Regulators and plants make their own decisions. We promise diligence, not outcomes.
- **Your information stays yours.** Client files are private, access is limited to your consultants, and we never sell data.

## Who we work with
- **Commercial operators.** Licensed cultivators, processors, and vertically integrated companies that need fixes before inspectors find problems.
- **Dispensaries & retail.** Storefronts that need tighter inventory, better staff training, and cleaner reconciliation.
- **New license holders.** Teams that just received a license and need SOPs, systems, and a build-out plan fast.

# Joel Perkins
**Agricultural Scientist, Formulation Specialist & Systems Architect**
Executive Consultant · Supply Chain Architect

Joel bridges agricultural biochemistry and large-scale operations. He designs nutrient programs and input strategies, vets suppliers, and structures the distribution and margin side of the business so the science pays for itself.

## Story
Joel came to agriculture from an unusual direction. He started in the California entertainment industry as a concert promoter running multiple live events every week, and was the lead vocalist and lyricist for the thrash metal band Six Pack of Doom. Running shows taught him logistics, crowds, and cash flow long before he ran a facility.

He moved into medical cannabis as manager of the Sespe Creek Collective in California, growing it into one of the state’s leading medical hubs, serving more than 10,000 registered patients, including oncology patients and wounded combat veterans.

Concern about agricultural contaminants like glyphosate pushed him into microbiology. He founded and ran a biological, fermentation-based fertilizer line that became a staple in the Humboldt market and was adopted by Driscoll’s growers for commercial berry production.

After serving as Chief Operating Officer of Primordial Solutions, Joel spent six years as a Division Head at Wilbur-Ellis, where he formulated botanical fertilizer lines and traveled internationally as a keynote speaker on plant metabolism. In Nevada he managed 24-hour, high-volume retail operations at Oasis Cannabis and led the restructuring of Bofloral’s US division into Valley of Fire Distribution. He is the formulator of Cowbell Cow Mag, an acetate-based calcium and magnesium supplement.

Today Joel is Head of Operations at Lake Leaf Cultivation, the tribal cannabis enterprise of the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe in Minnesota: a vertically integrated, 50,000-square-foot cultivation, manufacturing, and processing operation opened in April 2024, with more than 100 team members, wholesale relationships, and dispensaries in Onamia, Hinckley, and Isle.

- Head of Operations, Lake Leaf Cultivation (Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe, Minnesota)
- Founder, Valley of Fire Distribution (restructured from Bofloral’s US division)

- Retail operations, Oasis Cannabis (Nevada)
- Manager, Sespe Creek Collective (California, 10,000+ registered patients)
- Formulator, Cowbell Cow Mag
- Product development, Habitarium
- International keynote speaker on plant metabolism

## Specialties
- **Acetate-based nutrient strategies.** Joel pioneered commercial use of potassium and calcium acetate, which give the plant carbon in its most accessible form as a direct Acetyl-CoA precursor, to support metabolism, resin, and terpene production. - **Biological fertilizers & fermentation.** Microbial and fermentation-based inputs, how to brew and apply them consistently, and how to keep them from becoming a contamination source.

Treat every facility like a live lab. Change one variable, measure it honestly, and keep what works.

# How an engagement runs

Every engagement moves through these stages and is documented as it goes. You own the final record.

**1. Initial Problem**
What is actually happening, in your words and in the data, before anyone assumes a cause.

**2. Investigation**
Walk-throughs, photos, logs, lab results, plumbing, and paperwork. We collect evidence first.

**3. Idea**
Candidate explanations, ranked by likelihood and by how cheaply each can be tested.

**4. Proposed Fix**
A specific change with an owner, a cost, and what we expect to see if it works.

**5. Implementation**
The change is made, with your team, and every step is written down.

**6. Validation**
We measure whether it worked against the expectation we set before we started.

**7. Backup Plan**
What we do if it did not work, or if conditions change next month.

**8. Cross-Correlation**
How the finding touches agriculture, engineering, compliance, technology, and the business, so lessons travel.

**9. Final Report**
A written record you own: sources, decisions, results, and version history.

**10. Follow-Up**
A scheduled check-in to confirm the fix held and to catch the next issue early.

# Total THC: what it is and how to calculate it
Why labs report THCA separately, where the 0.877 factor comes from, and how to check a certificate of analysis yourself.

**Category:** Compliance · **Jurisdiction:** Federal & multi-state · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Dusty McLean
**Tags:** THC, THCA, lab results, hemp, COA, potency

## The short version

Raw plant material contains mostly THCA, the acid form of THC. Heat converts THCA into Δ9-THC by removing a carboxyl group, a process called decarboxylation. Total THC estimates how much Δ9-THC the material could contain once that happens.

The common formula is Total THC = (THCA × 0.877) + Δ9-THC.

## Where 0.877 comes from

When THCA loses its carboxyl group as carbon dioxide, the molecule gets lighter. The molar mass of Δ9-THC (about 314.5 g/mol) divided by the molar mass of THCA (about 358.5 g/mol) is about 0.877. So one milligram of THCA can become at most about 0.877 milligrams of THC.

## Checking a certificate of analysis

- Confirm the sample ID and batch number match your records.
- Check that results are on the basis your rules require, usually dry weight for hemp.
- Recalculate Total THC from the THCA and Δ9-THC lines and compare with the lab’s total.
- Look for the lab’s measurement uncertainty. A result near a legal limit may be treated differently depending on how uncertainty is applied.
- Keep the COA with the batch record for as long as your rules require.

## Why it matters for hemp

Under the federal hemp rule, a hemp sample is tested for total THC on a dry-weight basis, and material above the acceptable level must be remediated or disposed of under the rule’s procedures. Federal legislation enacted in November 2025 also changes the statutory hemp definition to a total-THC basis and limits THC in finished products, with an effective date in November 2026. Confirm the current status with USDA and your state before relying on any threshold.

## Try it

Use the Total THC calculator in Resources to run the numbers from your own COA.

How systems like Metrc and BioTrack work, and the daily habits that keep physical inventory and the system in agreement.

messages:
# Heavy metals: where they come from and how to keep them out
Cannabis readily takes up metals from its environment. Here is how to find and reduce the sources.

**Category:** Cultivation · **Jurisdiction:** General · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Joel Perkins
**Tags:** heavy metals, lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury, inputs, COA

## Why cannabis is sensitive

Cannabis is efficient at pulling minerals, including metals, out of soil and water. It has even been studied for cleaning contaminated soil. That is a liability for a crop that will be consumed.

## What labs usually test

State panels commonly include arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury. Some states test more. Check your state’s panel and action limits.

## Common sources

- Native soil, fill, or amendments from unknown origin
- Source water, especially well water
- Mined mineral inputs and some phosphate fertilizers
- Low-quality supplements and “organic” products without documentation
- Equipment: galvanized or soldered metal in contact with nutrient solution

## Reducing risk

- Ask every input supplier for a recent certificate of analysis that includes heavy metals.
- Test your source water and your media before the first run.
- Keep a supplier file with lot numbers so a bad result can be traced.
- Change one input at a time, so you can tell which one moved a result.

## Sources

# Integrated pest management that a crew will actually follow

**Category:** Cultivation · **Jurisdiction:** General · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Danny Davis
**Tags:** IPM, pests, russet mites, spider mites, powdery mildew, scouting

## Prevention first

- Quarantine new plants and cuttings before they enter production.
- Control entry: dedicated footwear, clean clothing, and room order from clean to dirty.
- Keep environment in range. Many pathogens follow humidity and stagnant air.

## Scout on a schedule

Assign rooms and days. Check leaf undersides, new growth, and sticky traps, and log what you see even when it is nothing. A log of “clean” is what makes the first sighting meaningful.

## Identify before you spray

Russet and broad mites are too small to see clearly without magnification; a 60× loupe or a digital microscope helps. Twisted or glossy new growth with no visible pests is a reason to look closer, not a reason to guess. Get an identification before you choose a control.

## Controls and compliance

Only use products your state allows for cannabis, and record every application with product, lot, rate, area, and applicator. Residue testing will find what the log does not mention.

messages:
# Why your far emitters starve: friction loss and the 45-degree rule
Every fitting costs pressure. How to lay out irrigation so the last plant gets what the first one does.

**Category:** Facility · **Jurisdiction:** General · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Danny Davis
**Tags:** irrigation, plumbing, pressure, pumps, fittings, 45 degree

## The problem

Water loses pressure to friction as it moves through pipe and especially through fittings. Sharp turns cause turbulence. Add enough of them and the plants at the end of a line get less water and nutrient than the ones near the pump.

## The 45-degree rule

Where a run needs to change direction, a long-sweep bend or a pair of 45-degree fittings usually loses less pressure than a single short-radius 90-degree elbow. Fewer abrupt turns means more even delivery and less work for the pump.

## Other checks

- Size main lines for your peak flow, not your average.
- Loop or center-feed long runs so pressure is balanced.
- Use pressure-compensating emitters where elevation or run length varies.
- Measure: catch emitter output in cups across the room and compare volumes.
- Install a pressure gauge after the filter, and log the reading.

## Sources
- USDA NRCS National Engineering Handbook, Part 623: Irrigation: <https://directives.nrcs.usda.gov/>

# Tissue culture basics for cannabis operators
What a tissue culture program does, what a small lab needs, and why clean stock matters.

**Category:** Cultivation · **Jurisdiction:** General · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Danny Davis
**Tags:** tissue culture, micropropagation, clean stock, HLVd, genetics, lab

## Why operators invest in it

Mother plants accumulate pests, pathogens, and viroids over time. Tissue culture lets you keep genetics in small sterile vessels, test them, and regenerate clean plants, which protects a library of cultivars in far less space.

## The stages

- Initiation: a small piece of clean tissue is placed on sterile media.
- Multiplication: shoots are divided and grown on.
- Rooting: shoots are moved to media that encourages roots.
- Acclimatization: plantlets are hardened off for the grow room.

## What a starter lab needs

- A clean room with controlled entry
- A laminar flow hood
- A way to sterilize media and tools, such as an autoclave or pressure sterilizer
- Media ingredients and a log for every batch
- Shelving with controlled light and temperature
- Training in aseptic technique, which matters more than any equipment

## Testing

Pair the program with pathogen testing, such as for hop latent viroid, so the stock you preserve is actually clean.

messages:
# Vapor pressure deficit (VPD) in plain language
Temperature and humidity together decide how hard a plant transpires. Here is how to read VPD.

**Category:** Cultivation · **Jurisdiction:** General · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Danny Davis
**Tags:** VPD, humidity, temperature, environment, HVAC

## What it is

VPD is the difference between how much moisture the air could hold at a given temperature and how much it actually holds. Higher VPD pulls water from leaves faster; lower VPD slows transpiration and can favor mold.

## How it is calculated

Saturation vapor pressure (kPa) ≈ 0.6108 × e^(17.27 × T ÷ (T + 237.3)), where T is in °C. VPD = saturation pressure × (1 − RH ÷ 100). Using leaf temperature instead of air temperature gives a better picture of what the plant feels.

## Using it

Targets vary by stage and cultivar. Watch the trend overnight as well as during the day; many problems start when lights go off and humidity spikes. The VPD calculator in Resources will run the numbers.

## Sources
- FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Chapter 3 (vapor pressure equations): <https://www.fao.org/4/x0490e/x0490e07.htm>

**Category:** Technology · **Jurisdiction:** General · **Reviewed:** 2026-10-21 · **Author:** Danny Davis

- Everything on one flat network with the office laptops
- Remote access through ports opened on the router

## What goes wrong

Drying too fast locks in harshness and drives off terpenes. Drying too slow or too wet invites mold and microbial failures. Both are common and both are preventable.

## Measure it

- Log room temperature and humidity throughout the dry.
- Weigh sample branches daily to track moisture loss.
- Use water activity, not just feel, to decide when product is ready. Some states set water-activity limits.
- Record the conditions for every batch so you can repeat a good one.

Many growers start near 60°F and 60% relative humidity in the dry room and adjust from there. Treat that as a starting point, not a rule.

channels.topic: Total THC and VPD formulas, worked examples, and links to the calculators.
messages:
# Calculators

## Total THC
**Total THC = (THCA × 0.877) + Δ9-THC**
Use the THCA and Δ9-THC values from your certificate of analysis, both in percent. For mg/g, divide by 10 to get percent. Multiply percent by 10 for mg per gram.

Example: THCA 0.25% and Δ9-THC 0.05% gives (0.25 × 0.877) + 0.05 = **0.269%**.
0.3% is the federal hemp threshold. Use your own rule's limit.
Calculator: <https://r3dconsulting.com/resources/total-thc>

## VPD (vapor pressure deficit)
Saturation vapor pressure, in kPa, at temperature T in °C: **SVP = 0.6108 × e^(17.27 × T ÷ (T + 237.3))**
- Actual vapor pressure = SVP(air) × RH ÷ 100
- Air VPD = SVP(air) − actual vapor pressure
- Leaf VPD = SVP(leaf) − actual vapor pressure, where leaf temperature = air temperature + leaf offset (often around 2 °F cooler)

Guide bands (leaf VPD): Propagation 0.4–0.8 kPa · Vegetative 0.8–1.2 kPa · Flower 1.2–1.6 kPa
Calculator: <https://r3dconsulting.com/resources/vpd>

Background: {#knowledge-base} (search `total thc` or `vpd`).

Each post below is one possible outcome of the decision tree on our website. Read the path at the top of each post to see the symptoms that lead there, or use the interactive version: <https://r3dconsulting.com/resources/troubleshooter>

## The first question

messages:
# Sanitation & Cleaning
**Applies to:** Cannabis cultivation, Processing / manufacturing, Dispensary / retail, Hemp producer

## Purpose
Keep work areas, equipment, and surfaces clean to prevent contamination of plants and product.

## Scope
All rooms, equipment, and surfaces at [Facility].

## Responsibilities
- [Owner] maintains the cleaning schedule and verifies completion.
- Every employee cleans their work area at the end of each task and shift.

## Procedure
1. Post the cleaning schedule in each room listing surfaces, frequency, method, and approved cleaning agents.
2. Before cleaning, put on the required protective equipment and remove product from the area.
3. Remove debris, then clean surfaces with detergent and water before sanitizing.
4. Apply the approved sanitizer at the label concentration and contact time.
5. Clean tools and equipment between rooms or batches to prevent cross-contamination.
6. Record the date, time, area, agent used, and initials on the cleaning log.
7. Report any damage, pests, mold, or leaks to [Owner] immediately.

## Records to keep
- Cleaning log
- Safety data sheets for every chemical used
- Corrective-action notes

messages:
# A new cultivation licensee six weeks from its first inspection
**Client type:** Newly licensed indoor cultivator
**Team:** Dusty McLean, Danny Davis
**Areas:** Commercial Facility Audits, Technology & Business Systems

## Initial Problem
The team had a license, a building, and a binder of template SOPs, but no one had walked the facility against the rules.

## Investigation
Mock inspection of every room, review of each SOP against the current regulations, and a test of the visitor log, camera coverage, and waste process.

## Idea
Most gaps were procedural, not physical. A few were physical: camera blind spots and a drain without a backflow device.

## Proposed Fix
Rewrite SOPs with the staff who do the work, add two cameras, fix the drain, and set up a daily log routine.

## Implementation
SOPs drafted, walked, and signed off room by room. Training recorded for every employee.

## Validation
A second mock inspection two weeks later with a fresh findings list.

## Backup Plan
Items that could not be fixed in time were documented with a corrective-action plan and dates.

## Cross-Correlation
The drain finding fed into the irrigation review; the camera gaps fed into the network security plan.

## Final Report
Findings, fixes, photos, signed training records, and revision history delivered to the client portal.

## Follow-Up
Monthly compliance check under a Tier 1 retainer.

-# Illustrative scenario, not a client result.

posts.title: Plants at the far end of every row underperforming
messages:
# Plants at the far end of every row underperforming
**Client type:** Commercial indoor cultivator
**Team:** Danny Davis, Joel Perkins, Dusty McLean
**Areas:** Cultivation & Processing, Commercial Facility Audits

## Initial Problem
The last third of each row ran smaller and showed deficiency symptoms, even though every plant was on the same feed.

## Investigation
Catch-cup tests at every emitter, pressure readings along each line, feed and runoff EC and pH logs, and a look at the plumbing layout.

## Idea
Pressure loss from a long run with many sharp elbows meant far emitters delivered less volume.

## Proposed Fix
Re-plumb with 45-degree fittings and a center feed, add a pressure gauge after the filter, and keep the feed recipe unchanged so the effect could be isolated.

## Implementation
One room re-plumbed first as a test, with the crew trained on the new layout.

## Validation
Emitter volumes compared before and after, plus plant measurements over the next run.

## Backup Plan
Pressure-compensating emitters if re-plumbing alone did not balance the room.

## Cross-Correlation
Once delivery was even, the feed program could be tuned; sensor alerts were added for pressure drops.

## Final Report
Before-and-after data, the new plumbing diagram, and an updated irrigation SOP.

## Follow-Up
Roll-out to the remaining rooms on the client’s schedule.

-# Illustrative scenario, not a client result.

posts.title: A hemp producer worried about pre-harvest testing
messages:
# A hemp producer worried about pre-harvest testing
**Client type:** Licensed hemp producer
**Team:** Dusty McLean, Joel Perkins
**Areas:** Agriculture & Formulation, Technology & Business Systems

## Initial Problem
In-house test results were creeping toward the limit as harvest approached, and the official sampling window was close.

## Investigation
Review of COAs and the lab’s reporting basis, recalculation of Total THC, cultivar history, and the planned harvest date.

## Idea
Results were trending up with maturity. Harvest timing and sampling date were the controllable variables.

## Proposed Fix
Schedule sampling and harvest together, track Total THC weekly on a shared dashboard, and prepare a documented remediation plan in advance.

## Implementation
Weekly testing schedule, Total THC tracking, and a written remediation SOP ready before sampling.

## Validation
Official results compared with in-house trend data.

## Backup Plan
If a lot tested high, follow the pre-approved remediation or disposal procedure and document every step.

## Cross-Correlation
Cultivar selection for the next season was informed by the THC trend data.

## Final Report
Testing timeline, calculations, the remediation SOP, and recommendations for next season.

## Follow-Up
Pre-season planning call before the next planting.

-# Illustrative scenario, not a client result.

posts.title: A dispensary with recurring inventory variances
messages:
# A dispensary with recurring inventory variances
**Client type:** Single-location dispensary
**Team:** Dusty McLean, Danny Davis
**Areas:** Dispensary & Retail Operations, Technology & Business Systems

## Initial Problem
Month-end counts never matched the tracking system, and staff were adjusting numbers to make them agree.

## Investigation
Transaction review, observation of receiving and sales, scale checks, and interviews with each shift.

## Idea
Receiving was recorded late, and one scale drifted. Adjustments were hiding the root causes.

## Proposed Fix
Record receiving at the dock, calibrate and log scales daily, require a reason for every adjustment, and add daily cycle counts.

## Implementation
New receiving and adjustment SOPs, staff training, and a simple daily count sheet.

## Validation
Variance tracked weekly for two months.

## Backup Plan
Escalation procedure for any unexplained variance, including when to notify the regulator.

## Cross-Correlation
Product training for staff was added after the review showed frequent mis-rings between similar products.

## Final Report
Variance trend, SOPs, training records, and a dashboard for the manager.

## Follow-Up
Quarterly reconciliation check.

-# Illustrative scenario, not a client result.

# Partner guide

Everyone with the **Root3D Partner** role (Dusty, Danny, Joel, and Hunter) is a server admin and can edit channels, post anywhere, pin, and manage roles.

## Give someone access
Right-click their name → **Roles** → add **Client** or **Insider**. Remove the role to take access away.

- **Client**: active consulting clients. Clients also see Insider channels.

## Make a private client room
Right-click the **CLIENTS** category → **Create Channel** → name it `client-<company>` → turn on **Private Channel** → add the client and the partners on the account.

## Post a briefing
Post in the Insider channel that fits, start with a one-line bold headline, and add the date and your sources. Draft in {#content-drafts} first if you want a second set of eyes. Use **Publish** in {#announcements} to push news to followers.

## Add to the Knowledge Base
The public library mirrors <https://r3dconsulting.com/knowledge-base>. Add new articles on the website first, then run the Discord builder again (see the handbook). It only adds what is missing.

## Calls
Clients choose Zoom, Discord, or Signal when they book. For Zoom, use the saved Manna Zoom room link in the portal (it is shared and open 24 hours, so check no one else is using it). For Discord, use Consult Room 1 or 2. No phone numbers.

## Moderation
Delete rule-breaking posts, and time out or ban repeat offenders (right-click the user). Discord system notices go to {#mod-log}.
